lead: An adsorbent can meet the fluid in three ways. In stagewise contact, powdered adsorbent is stirred into the liquid and filtered off. In a moving bed, granules travel down a column against the rising fluid. In a fixed bed, the fluid flows through stationary granules until the bed is full and must be regenerated. The fixed bed is the commonest; its breakthrough curve tells the operator when to switch.
prereq: You need the Freundlich and Langmuir isotherms from Adsorption equilibria: Langmuir and Freundlich isotherms.

blocks.text: In one stage, W kg of fresh adsorbent is mixed with V of liquid at C<sub>0</sub> and leaves in equilibrium with the final liquid C<sub>1</sub>. The solute balance V(C<sub>0</sub> − C<sub>1</sub>) = W q(C<sub>1</sub>) is a straight operating line of slope −V/W on the q–C diagram; where it cuts the isotherm is the result. The adsorbent ends in equilibrium with the cleanest liquid, so one stage is wasteful when C<sub>1</sub> must be low.

Cross-current: the liquid is treated twice, each time with fresh adsorbent, and the spent adsorbent is filtered off after each stage. The first stage then works at a higher concentration, and so at a higher loading. For a Freundlich isotherm the least total adsorbent comes from choosing the middle concentration C1 to satisfy (C1/C2)1/n − (1/n)(C0/C1) = 1 − 1/n.

Counter-current: fresh adsorbent meets the cleanest liquid in the last stage, then is moved to the first stage to meet the incoming feed, where it leaves loaded almost to q(C0). The balances are V(C0 − C2) = W q1 overall and V(C1 − C2) = W q2 for the last stage, with q1 = q(C1) and q2 = q(C2).

A moving bed carries the counter-current idea to a column: granules enter at the top, fall slowly as a dense bed against the rising fluid, leave loaded at the bottom and go to a regenerator before returning. It acts like many counter-current stages, but the granules wear as they move. Today the same effect is obtained without moving solid in the simulated moving bed: a ring of fixed beds in which rotary valves move the feed and product points one bed along at set times, used to separate p-xylene and to purify sugars.

sections.h3: Fixed bed: zones and the breakthrough curve

blocks.text: Feed at C0 enters a bed of fresh adsorbent. The grains near the inlet load first and soon reach equilibrium with C0: the saturated zone. Ahead of it is the mass-transfer zone (MTZ), a band in which the fluid concentration falls from C0 to nearly zero and the adsorbent is partly loaded. Below it the adsorbent is still clean.

When the front of the MTZ reaches the outlet, the exit concentration C starts to rise. The plot of C/C0 against time (or volume treated) is the breakthrough curve, usually S-shaped. The break point tb is the time at which C reaches the highest level the product may contain, often C/C0 = 0.05 or 0.10; the bed is switched there. Exhaustion is at C/C0 ≈ 0.95.
t<sub>s</sub> = ∫<sub>0</sub><sup>∞</sup> (1 − C/C<sub>0</sub>) dt      held = C<sub>0</sub>Qt<sub>s</sub>      LUB = H(1 − t<sub>b</sub>/t<sub>s</sub>)
blocks.where: Q is the volumetric feed rate and H the bed height. t<sub>s</sub> is the stoichiometric time: the time an ideal bed with a vertical front would last. The area above the curve up to t<sub>b</sub> gives the solute held at the break point. LUB, the length of unused bed, is the part of the bed still unused at the break point (about half the MTZ). For a new design with the same fluid velocity and particle size the LUB stays the same, so a longer bed is H<sub>new</sub> = H<sub>used</sub> + LUB.

items: Flow rate. A higher velocity brings solute faster and gives less contact time, so tb comes earlier, the MTZ widens and the LUB grows.
Particle size. Smaller grains shorten the pore path, so the curve sharpens, at the price of a higher pressure drop.
Bed height. The LUB stays nearly fixed, so a taller bed uses a larger fraction of its adsorbent before the break point.

Isotherm shape. A favourable isotherm makes the front self-sharpening: the dilute part of the front is held more strongly and moves slower than the concentrated part, so the front keeps a constant shape. An unfavourable isotherm spreads the front as it travels.

blocks.text: Plants run two or more beds, one adsorbing while another is regenerated by hot gas or steam (temperature swing), lower pressure (pressure swing) or a solvent wash. In lead–lag operation two beds run in series, so the first can be run to exhaustion.

examples.question: 1000 L of wastewater containing 50 mg/L of phenol is to be reduced to 5 mg/L with powdered carbon whose isotherm is q = 8C<sup>0.5</sup> (q in mg/g, C in mg/L). Find the carbon needed (a) in one stage, (b) in two cross-current stages at the best intermediate concentration, (c) in two counter-current stages.
steps: (a) The carbon leaves at q(5) = 8 × 5<sup>0.5</sup> = 17.89 mg/g. Solute to remove = 1000 × (50 − 5) = 45 000 mg. W = 45 000/17.89 = 2516 g = 2.52 kg.

(c) Counter-current: (C<sub>0</sub> − C<sub>2</sub>)/q(C<sub>1</sub>) = (C<sub>1</sub> − C<sub>2</sub>)/q(C<sub>2</sub>), that is 45/(8√C<sub>1</sub>) = (C<sub>1</sub> − 5)/17.89. By trial, C<sub>1</sub> = 25.09 mg/L: left side 45/40.07 = 1.123, right side 20.09/17.89 = 1.123.
W = 1000 × 45/40.07 = 1123 g = 1.12 kg. The carbon leaves stage 1 at 40.07 mg/g, more than twice the single-stage loading.
examples.answer: One stage 2.52 kg; two cross-current stages 1.67 kg (946 + 723 g, C<sub>1</sub> = 17.9 mg/L); two counter-current stages 1.12 kg, less than half the single-stage carbon.

examples.question: A carbon bed 0.60 m high holding 1500 g of carbon treats 2 L/min of water containing 80 mg/L of a dye. The exit concentration is: t (min) 0, 20, 30, 40, 50, 60, 70, 80, 90, 100, 110 and C/C<sub>0</sub> 0, 0.01, 0.05, 0.15, 0.35, 0.60, 0.80, 0.92, 0.97, 0.99, 1.00. Take the break point at C/C<sub>0</sub> = 0.05. Find the loading at the break point, the saturation loading, the LUB, and the break time of a 1.2 m bed at the same velocity.
steps: Break point t<sub>b</sub> = 30 min. Area above the curve to 30 min by trapezoids: (1 + 0.99)/2 × 20 + (0.99 + 0.95)/2 × 10 = 19.9 + 9.7 = 29.6 min.
Dye held at the break point = 80 mg/L × 2 L/min × 29.6 min = 4736 mg, so q<sub>b</sub> = 4736/1500 = 3.16 mg/g.
Whole area: add 9.0, 7.5, 5.25, 3.0, 1.4, 0.55, 0.2 and 0.05 min for the later intervals: t<sub>s</sub> = 56.55 min. Dye held at saturation = 80 × 2 × 56.55 = 9048 mg, q<sub>sat</sub> = 6.03 mg/g.
Fraction of the capacity used at the break point = 4736/9048 = 52 %. LUB = 0.60 × (1 − 30/56.55) = 0.60 × 0.469 = 0.28 m.
1.2 m bed: t<sub>s</sub> doubles to 113.1 min and the LUB stays 0.28 m, so t<sub>b</sub> = 113.1 × (1.2 − 0.28)/1.2 = 86.5 min, and 77 % of the bed is used at the break point.
examples.answer: q<sub>b</sub> = 3.16 mg/g, q<sub>sat</sub> = 6.03 mg/g, LUB = 0.28 m; a 1.2 m bed reaches its break point at about 86 min instead of 30 min.

traps: The loading at the break point is not C<sub>0</sub>Qt<sub>b</sub>/W (3.20 mg/g here): that assumes nothing at all left the bed before t<sub>b</sub>. Integrate the area above the curve.
An early break point with a slow, spread-out curve means a long LUB and a poorly used bed, not a well-used one.
A favourable isotherm sharpens the front; an unfavourable one spreads it, even with fast mass transfer.

quiz.q: Define the break point and the mass-transfer zone of a fixed bed.
quiz.a: The break point is the time when the exit concentration reaches the allowed limit (often C/C<sub>0</sub> = 0.05). The mass-transfer zone is the band of bed in which the fluid concentration falls from C<sub>0</sub> to nearly zero.

quiz.q: Why does two-stage counter-current contact need less adsorbent than one stage for the same final concentration?
quiz.a: In one stage the adsorbent ends in equilibrium with the cleanest liquid, so its loading is low. Counter-current, the adsorbent leaves the stage where the feed enters and loads nearly to q(C<sub>0</sub>), so each gram carries more solute.

quiz.q: A bed gives t<sub>b</sub> = 40 min and t<sub>s</sub> = 50 min at H = 1.0 m. Find the LUB and the height needed for t<sub>b</sub> = 80 min at the same velocity.
quiz.a: LUB = 1.0 × (1 − 40/50) = 0.20 m. The used part moves 0.80 m in 40 min, so 80 min needs 1.60 m used plus 0.20 m: H = 1.80 m.

quiz.q: Why do favourable isotherms give a self-sharpening front in a fixed bed?
quiz.a: On a favourable isotherm, q/C is larger at low C, so the dilute leading edge of the front is held more strongly and moves slower than the concentrated part behind it. The back catches up with the front, and dispersion is balanced, so the front keeps a constant shape.

quiz.q: With q = 8C<sup>0.5</sup> and feed at 50 mg/L, what is the highest loading carbon can leave a counter-current system with?
quiz.a: q(C<sub>0</sub>) = 8 × 50<sup>0.5</sup> = 56.6 mg/g, reached only with infinitely many stages.

beyond: Not for the exam. Breakthrough curves are now fitted with simple models such as Thomas, Bohart–Adams and Yoon–Nelson, or simulated by solving the column mass balance with a linear driving force for the grain. Rapid small-scale column tests let water utilities test carbon in hours instead of months. Search for rapid small-scale column test and simulated moving bed.

figure.caption: The measured breakthrough curve of the worked example. The shaded area above the curve up to the break point (30 min) is the dye held then; the whole area above the curve gives the stoichiometric time 56.6 min. At the break point the bed is used to 0.32 m and the last 0.28 m, the length of unused bed, is still partly fresh.
